course.title: HTML
course.description: A deeply researched practical HTML course progressing from document syntax and semantic structure through links, media, tables, forms, metadata, native interactive elements, parsing, accessibility, security, performance, advanced platform markup, validation, and a complete real-world documentation portal.
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with files, folders, and a text editor.
Ability to open a local HTML file in a modern web browser.
No prior HTML programming experience is required.
learningOutcomes: Create complete standards-based HTML documents with correct metadata and language declarations.
Design semantic document structures with appropriate headings, landmarks, sections, articles, lists, and text semantics.
Build meaningful navigation, links, fragments, downloads, and safe external link relationships.
Embed images and media with contextual alternatives, responsive sources, captions, and fallbacks.
Build accessible data tables with captions, headers, scopes, and explicit relationships.
Build usable forms with labels, fieldsets, native input types, autocomplete, constraints, and deliberate submission semantics.
Use metadata, language, direction, and resource relationships appropriately.
Use native interactive HTML features such as details, dialog, popover, progress, meter, hidden, and inert when appropriate.
Embed external content with iframe titles, sandbox restrictions, and fallback paths.
Explain HTML parsing and debug differences between source markup and the live DOM.
Apply native semantic HTML and keyboard-first practices as an accessibility foundation.
Recognize HTML injection and XSS risks and apply safe data, URL, sanitization, and sandbox boundaries.
Use performance and loading hints selectively and explain their tradeoffs.
Understand template, slot, custom-element markup, and declarative shadow roots at the HTML/Web Components boundary.
Validate, test, audit, and iteratively improve a multi-page HTML project.

notes.text: HTML is a document language

HTML describes a document using elements and attributes. A browser parses the delivered text into a document tree and uses the resulting semantics when exposing the page to users and platform features. CSS primarily controls presentation, while JavaScript adds programmable behavior.

HTML Course

HTML gives this content structure and meaning.
A semantic element should be selected for what the content means, not merely how it looks.
items: Elements form the document tree.
Attributes add information to elements.
Semantic HTML provides a useful baseline for accessibility and tooling.

lessons.title: Form Anatomy and Submission
lessons.description: Understand action, method, name, and successful form submission.

notes.text: Form Anatomy and Submission

The form element groups controls and defines submission behavior. GET is common for retrieval such as search; POST is common for state-changing or body-submitted data. The server remains responsible for validation and authorization.
<form action="/search" method="get"><label for="q">Search</label><input id="q" name="q" type="search"><button type="submit">Search</button></form>

text: Forms are data interfaces with explicit control names and submission semantics.
items: Forms are data interfaces with explicit control names and submission semantics.

notes.text: Constraint Validation
HTML constraint validation can reject invalid submissions and provide immediate feedback. It is not a security boundary because clients can be bypassed or manipulated; servers must validate again.
<input name="username" required minlength="3" maxlength="30" pattern="[A-Za-z0-9_]+">

text: HTML constraints improve UX; server-side validation remains mandatory.
items: HTML constraints improve UX; server-side validation remains mandatory.

practicals.output: The browser can provide validation feedback, while the server remains responsible for trust.

quiz.question: Can native validation replace server-side validation?
quiz.explanation: Client validation can be bypassed and cannot establish trust.

summary: HTML constraint validation can reject invalid submissions and provide immediate feedback. It is not a security boundary because clients can be bypassed or manipulated; servers must validate again.

notes.text: CSP as Defense in Depth

Content Security Policy restricts resource loading and certain script capabilities. It can reduce impact from some injection attacks but does not replace contextual output encoding or sanitization. A production CSP should be designed for the actual application and tested.
<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'">

text: Security is layered across application and browser boundaries.
items: Security is layered across application and browser boundaries.

summary: Content Security Policy restricts resource loading and certain script capabilities. It can reduce impact from some injection attacks but does not replace contextual output encoding or sanitization. A production CSP should be designed for the actual application and tested.

lessons.title: preload and prefetch
lessons.description: Use resource hints with evidence and restraint.

notes.text: preload and prefetch
preload signals that the current page expects a resource soon; prefetch suggests a resource that may be useful for a future navigation. Incorrect hints can compete with more important network work.

<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/course.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>
<link rel="prefetch" href="/next-page.html">

text: Resource hints are strong signals; use them only when justified.

project.name: Accessible Training Documentation Portal
project.description: Build a multi-page HTML-first technical training documentation portal demonstrating semantic structure, navigation, responsive media, data tables, accessible forms, native interactive elements, metadata, and secure embedded content. The project uses neutral sample content and contains no personal information.
steps: Create index.html, course.html, catalog.html, enrollment.html, and preview.html.
Give every page a complete document structure, title, charset, viewport, and lang.
Add a consistent navigation landmark and skip link.
Build the home page with a semantic article and figure.
Build the course page with responsive picture, captioned video, progress, FAQ, and popover help.
Build the catalog page with caption, thead/tbody/tfoot, row and column headers, and an aggregate row.
Build the enrollment page with fieldsets, legends, labels, named controls, autocomplete, native constraints, and consent.
Build the preview page with a restrictive sandboxed iframe and direct fallback link.
Validate links, image alternatives, form relationships, and table relationships.
Review untrusted content and URL boundaries before deployment.
Run conformance, keyboard, accessibility, security, and performance checks.
Fix all discovered issues and repeat the audit.

project.explanation: The final project is HTML-first. Each page has a complete document structure, language metadata, navigation, and a unique main region. The course page integrates responsive media, captions, progress, disclosure, and popover; the catalog demonstrates accessible table relationships; enrollment demonstrates grouped forms, labels, autocomplete, constraints, and consent; and preview demonstrates a restrictive iframe sandbox with a direct alternative. Security-sensitive responsibilities such as server validation, URL validation, sanitization, and production CSP remain explicit application concerns. Asset paths in the sample code are implementation inputs and must point to real deployed resources before shipping.
